props.title: Westworld
props.initialSlug: Robots run amok in deadly theme park nightmare

sections.content: Westworld revolutionized sci-fi by introducing the first CGI effects in feature film history and establishing the "killer robot" template that would influence everything from The Terminator (1984) to Ex Machina (2014). Michael Crichton's directorial debut eerily predicted AI rebellion decades before it became a mainstream concern, following two visitors (Richard Benjamin and James Brolin) at a high-tech adult theme park where the robotic hosts, led by Yul Brynner's relentless Gunslinger, turn deadly. The film's DNA is clearly visible in Crichton's later Jurassic Park (1993) - both feature leisure attractions where corporate hubris leads to technological catastrophe.

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond its immediate sequels. AI: Artificial Intelligence (2001) explores similar questions of machine consciousness and human responsibility toward our creations. The HBO series Westworld (2016-2022) expands the original's premise into a philosophically complex examination of consciousness, free will, and what defines humanity. Even Free Guy (2021) owes a debt to the concept of AI characters becoming self-aware within manufactured worlds. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Robot Cinema

Westworld's portrayal of humanoid robots marked a crucial shift from the clunky mechanoids of Forbidden Planet (1956) and The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951). Its sophisticated androids, indistinguishable from humans until they malfunction, set the stage for films like Ex Machina (2014) and Prometheus (2012), where the line between human and machine becomes increasingly blurred. The film's theme park setting and corporate negligence storyline also influenced disaster films like Jurassic World (2015) and Deep Blue Sea (1999).
